newsitem.title: USA: Enron posts second-quarter loss, lowers earnings target.
newsitem.headline: Enron posts second-quarter loss, lowers earnings target.

text.p: Enron Corp. Tuesday posted a $420 million second-quarter net loss stemming from costs of settling a natural gas contract dispute and a charge tied to its unprofitable gasoline-additives business.

The Houston-based energy giant also warned that sluggish oil and gas prices are not expected to offset hedging losses taken earlier in the year, pushing Enron shares lower and prompting analysts to trim earnings estimates for the year.
Enron's stock slid $1.25 to $39 on the New York Stock Exchange and was one of the day's most-active issues.
"While we're clearly not happy about reporting a loss of any magnitude ... we are extremely pleased with the significant progress we made during the quarter," Chairman Ken Lay said.

He was referring to Enron's settlement of the legal dispute with a consortium over gas supplies from the British North Sea and the recent completion of its $3 billion acquisition of Portland General Corp.

Enron posted a $1.71 a share loss in the second quarter, compared with profits of $117 million, or 46 cents a share, in the second quarter last year. Excluding the charges, Enron had operating income of $104 million in the second quarter, and revenues rose to $3.2 billion from $3.0 billion last year.

The company last month said it would take an after-tax charge of $450 million, or $1.81 a share, reflecting the full payment to a consortium to amend terms of a contract to buy gas from the J-Block field British North Sea.

Enron in 1992 agreed to pay a fixed price for the gas, but withheld payments and challenged the contract after market prices tumbled. With a London court poised to rule against it, Enron settled with Phillips Petroleum, British Gas and Agip.

One of the nation's largest independent oil and gas companies, Enron also took a one-time, after-tax charge of $74 million, or 30 cents a share, to reflect depressed gasoline-additive margins in the second quarter.

Enron, which has been shouldering costs of building a nationwide retail electric and gas franchise, plans to cut its losses in part by selling up to a 15 percent stake in a newly formed energy services business later this year, Lay said.

Enron Energy Services, which is poised to compete in the $300 billion a year U.S. electric and gas retail markets opening to competition beginning next year, racked up $25 million in losses in the second quarter.

"The Street is penalising Enron for spending $25 million a quarter to attempt to penetrate a $300 billion market," CS First Boston analyst Steven Parla said. "Interesting that no one else is spending significant sums to penetrate this market."

Enron's domestic power marketing business has emerged as the largest U.S. independent power wholesaler, selling 38.6 million megawatt hours in the second quarter versus 11 million megawatt hours in the second quarter of 1996.
The company expects to begin signing up customers this fall ahead of planned openings of retail electric markets in California and New England on Jan. 1, 1998.

With the release of its latest earnings, Enron cut its internal 1997 and 1998 earnings forecasts, prompting PaineWebber Inc. and CS First Boston in turn to lower their estimates for the oil and gas company.
PaineWebber cut its rating on Enron's stock to neutral from attractive. First Boston, however, continued to recommend buying the stock, saying it is expected to reach $50 a share.
To prop up its shares, the company's board approved a plan to buy back up to 10 million shares this year.

Separately, Enron said it holds the largest stake in the consortium that was the successful bidder in the privatisation of CEG, Rio de Janeiro's municipal gas distribution company, and Riogas, the gas distribution company in the interior of the state of Rio de Janeiro.
Enron said the winning bid for a 56.4 percent stake in CEG and a 75 percent stake in Riogas was about $576 million.
